docs.text: The Micro OS wiki ¶ Micro OS is a Linux-like kernel for small machines: one portable core, and a port per kind of machine. This wiki is the user guide - how to build the system, drive its shell, find a file, run a program, and fix what does not work. The canonical documents stay in docs/ : the architecture, the roadmap, the ABI and the decisions of the project. This wiki links to them rather than copying them, and when a page here and a document there disagree, the document is right. There is no Russian translation of the wiki yet; the canonical Russian documents are in docs/ru/ . Start here ¶ If you want to... The ABI is written down in docs/syscall-abi.md ; the wiki page is a guide to it, not a second copy. Serving the wiki as a site ¶ mkdocs.yml in the root of the repository is a draft of a site: it is not a part of the build and make ci does not need it. The pages are plain Markdown and GitHub renders them as they are. To serve them locally: python3 -m pip install --user mkdocs mkdocs-material mkdocs serve # http://127.0.0.1:8000 mkdocs build # writes site/, which is generated docs_dir is docs/wiki , and MkDocs reads this file as the home page of the site. The theme is material ; if mkdocs-material is not installed, replace theme: material with theme: readthedocs in mkdocs.yml and plain mkdocs serves the pages. The wiki links into the rest of docs/ on purpose, so a build may warn about targets that live outside the site; the links themselves are checked against the repository by the script below. Checking the links ¶ python3 tools/wiki_check.py # docs/wiki, every link and anchor python3 tools/wiki_check.py docs/wiki/shell.md # one page python3 tools/wiki_check.py --verbose # one line per page The script fails on a target that does not exist and on an anchor that no heading of the target file produces. It is run by hand today; the natural place for it is make integrity (or a step of make ci next to the other repository checks), which is a change of the Makefile and not a part of this wiki. What the wiki does not do ¶ The wiki does not replace the design documents, the ADRs or the phase reports: it explains how to use the system, not why it is shaped the way it is. It also does not promise what the tree does not do - a feature that is planned is marked as planned, and the roadmap is the place where its status is kept.

docs.text: Build and run ¶ Three builds come out of one tree, and each of them is a check of the portability as much as a product: Build What it produces Commands Directory host the unit tests and the simulator, as a Linux process make build , make test , make sim , make smoke build-host/ , build-asan/ , build-tsan/ x86-64 a bare-metal kernel and its loader, for QEMU make x86-build , make x86-run , make x86-smoke build-x86/ ESP32 the firmware of the board, through ESP-IDF v5.3 make idf-build , make idf-flash , make bundle build/ The null port ( ports/port_null ) has no build of its own: it is linked into the host build as microos_null_probe , and the link is the check. Dependencies ¶ Package Needed by Arch / CachyOS Debian / Ubuntu cmake , ninja every build cmake ninja cmake ninja-build gcc the host and x86 builds gcc gcc python3 the tools, the checks, ESP-IDF python python3 qemu-system-x86_64 running the x86-64 machine qemu-system-x86 qemu-system-x86 GTK backend of QEMU the window of make x86-run qemu-ui-gtk qemu-system-gui clang-format make format , the format check clang-format clang-format valgrind the cloud run of the tests, optional valgrind valgrind pyserial tools/console.py , tools/stream_console.py python3 -m pip install pyserial the same The packages of the last two columns are installed with sudo pacman -S --needed ... or sudo apt install ... . ESP-IDF is needed only for the board; it brings its own toolchain and Python environment. commands.md is the reference for the packages and for the variables that override the defaults. The host build ¶ make build # cmake -B build-host -S . -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug make test # build, then ctest: the unit tests and the null probe make test-asan # the same tests with the address and UB sanitizers make test-tsan # the same tests under the race detector make sim # build, then run build-host/ports/port_host/microos_sim make smoke # boot the simulator and check what it says The same by hand: cmake -B build-host -S . -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE = Debug cmake --build build-host ctest --test-dir build-host --output-on-failure build-host/ports/port_host/microos_sim The simulator is the whole system on a volume in a file: MicroFS, /proc , /dev , the configuration of /etc , the init scripts and the shell. The environment shapes it: Variable Meaning Default MICROOS_VOLUME the file of the MicroFS volume /tmp/microos-sim.img MICROOS_KV_DIR the directory of the key-value store /tmp/microos-kv MICROOS_SCREEN draw the console into this file instead of nowhere unset MICROOS_INPUT a script of button events for input unset make sim is interactive; make smoke ( tools/sim_smoke.py ) drives it with a list of commands and checks the transcript. make clean removes build-host/ and build-asan/ only: build-tsan/ and build/ stay. The x86-64 build ¶ make x86-build # the loader and the kernel, into build-x86/ make x86-run # a QEMU window: VGA text and the PS/2 keyboard make x86-run-serial # the same machine in a terminal (-nographic) make x86-smoke # boot and check the transcript, no window make x86-vga-smoke # check the screen and the keyboard without a display make x86-run-disk # the window with an 8 MB disk on the IDE channel make x86-run-disk-serial # the same disk in a terminal make x86-disk-smoke # two boots on one image: a file survives both The build is a CMake project of its own ( ports/port_x86_64 ), because the kernel there has no libc under it. The image is two files: build-x86/loader32.elf (a multiboot loader that QEMU takes with -kernel ) and build-x86/microos64.bin (the flat kernel image). The programs of /bin are built first ( hello.mox , crash.mox , fork.mox , badptr.mox ) and the kernel carries them as blobs, because it needs the bytes before it has a filesystem to read them from. The display backend is a package of its own in some distributions: the target asks QEMU for its list of backends first and prints the command to run when the one asked for is missing. make x86-run X86_DISPLAY=sdl picks SDL, and make x86-run-serial is the machine for a box without a display server at all. The disk is a raw image of 8 MB, made the first time it is needed ( tools/x86_disk_smoke.py --mkimage ) and kept in build-x86/disk.img . It is generated, not committed; make clean does not remove build-x86/ , so rm -rf build-x86 is the way to start over. The details are in the port's README, docs/ports/x86_64/README.md . The ESP32 build ¶ make idf-build finds ESP-IDF on its own, in this order: $IDF_PATH , a checkout beside the repository ( ../esp-idf ), then ~/esp/esp-idf . Point it elsewhere with IDF_EXPORT=/path/to/export.sh ; there is no need to source export.sh for the make idf-* targets. make idf-build # idf.py -D IDF_TARGET=esp32 build make idf-flash # flash over USB; make idf-flash IDF_PORT=/dev/ttyACM0 make idf-monitor # the serial monitor (leave with Ctrl+]) make idf-size # the size report of the firmware make bundle # build everything and collect dist/ for distribution A first checkout needs the target once. With ESP-IDF exported: idf.py set-target esp32 idf.py build idf.py -p /dev/ttyACM0 flash monitor idf.py menuconfig # the Micro OS Kconfig (components/drivers/Kconfig) idf.py erase-flash # wipes everything, MicroFS data included The board is on /dev/ttyACM0 and the port belongs to the group uucp : sudo gpasswd -a $USER uucp # log out and back in afterwards tools/device-test.sh builds, flashes and reads the console, and prints RESULT: PASS when the self test, the hardware doctor and the shell are up. The layout of the flash is in partitions.csv : factory 2 MB and MicroFS 5.75 MB, with no room for an OTA slot. The board's own README is docs/ports/esp32/README.md , the pins and quirks are in docs/ports/esp32/hardware.md . The checks around the builds ¶ make integrity # the bundle, the image headers, the partition table, git, hygiene, format make format # reformat the C sources with clang-format make ci # build, test, test-asan, test-tsan, smoke, [x86-smoke], integrity make ci runs the x86-64 smoke test when qemu-system-x86_64 is on PATH and says so when it is not. It does not build the firmware, and it does not run the VGA or disk smoke tests or the device test: those are separate commands. testing.md explains what each check proves. When the build stops ¶ troubleshooting.md is the table of the errors that happen most: ESP-IDF not found, a toolchain that the registry of ESP-IDF does not know, a QEMU without a display, /dev/ttyACM0 that belongs to somebody else, and the link errors of a stale build directory. docs.text: Files ¶ Micro OS has one filesystem of its own, MicroFS , two virtual filesystems, and a FAT12/16/32 volume it can both read and write. The root / is MicroFS on a block device; /proc and /dev are generated by the kernel. Everything a person writes at the console lands in MicroFS unless a FAT volume is mounted, and the configuration of /etc has a second copy in the store of the port, which is why a format does not have to lose it. The layout of the volume, the sections and the flags of a record are described in docs/memory.md ; this page is about using it. The tree after a boot ¶ The simulator, right after a boot (the board adds /log , x86-64 adds /bin ): microos> ls / / |-- etc/ | `-- init.d/ |-- proc/ | |-- version | |-- uptime | |-- meminfo | |-- tasks | |-- modules | |-- self/ | |-- 1/ | `-- ... `-- dev/ |-- tty0 `-- ... Path What it is / MicroFS on the volume of the port /etc the configuration: a file name is the key, its content the value /etc/init.d the scripts of the init process, one command per line /etc/fstab the volumes the boot mounts after the root, when the file is there /proc the kernel: version , uptime , meminfo , tasks , modules , one directory per task /dev the devices: tty0 , null , input and the ones the port adds /log on the board: start.log , the log of the boot /bin on x86-64: the programs the boot writes ( hello , crash , fork , badptr ) ls prints the tree below a path and takes no flags; stat is the detailed view of one object. MicroFS ¶ MicroFS is a consumer of blocks, not of a flash chip: the device under it is described by kernel/blockdev.h and registered by the port. On the board it is the mfs partition of the internal flash ( flash0 , 5.75 MB); in the simulator a file of the host ( file0 , 512 KB by default); on x86-64 the first partition of the ATA disk ( ata0p1 ) when one is attached, and a volume in the RAM ( ram0 , 512 KB) when it is not. A volume has three sections and a block is 1 KiB: Section Holds DATA the content of the files META the table of the records and the map of the free blocks INFO the header of the volume and the root record, in the last erase sector A record of today is 32 bytes: it keeps the type of the object, its mode and its owner in the upper bits of flags , and the two moments of a change ( mtime and ctime ) in the seconds of Unix after them. A volume of an older release has 16-byte records with no room for a time and mounts unchanged; its objects report zero, which is "unknown" (ADR 0013). The formatter asks for 256 records ( MFS_MOUNT_RECORDS ) and sizes META from the volume; the capacity is fixed at format time and cannot grow later. There is no journal : fsck reports the first problem it finds and does not repair, and a power cut in the middle of a write is a risk the tree knows about ( docs/debts.md ). The calls of the filesystem take one recursive lock, so two tasks can use the volume at the same time without corrupting it: each open file keeps its position in its descriptor, and the volume itself is one piece of state behind a mutex. The codes of the filesystem are translated into the codes of the system calls in one place, components/mfs/src/mfs_vfs.c . Working with files ¶ microos> write /hello.txt one two three 14 byte(s) written to /hello.txt microos> cat /hello.txt one two three microos> mkdir /data microos> df /data blocks: 482 of 487 free (1 KB each) inodes: 1274 of 1279 free microos> rm /hello.txt write replaces the file and appends a newline; the text is one line of at most 127 bytes. rm removes a file, not a directory, and there is no -r . df prints the free blocks and inodes of the filesystem of the path. stat shows the mode, the owner and the size; chmod and chown change the first two. A program asks for the moments of a change with statx (number 26 of the ABI) and microos_statx() in the library; a volume of version 1 has none, so the two times come back as zero and not as 1970. The rules are in kernel-abi.md and in docs/syscall-abi.md : one user (uid 0), no root bypass, and a zero mode means "this record predates the modes", so chmod 000 is refused. mkfs and fsck ¶ microos> mkfs -y mkfs: the volume is formatted mkfs -y unmounts / , formats the volume and mounts it again. Without -y it does nothing but print its usage; with -y everything in MicroFS is gone. It is registered on the board ( main/src/main.c ) and in the simulator ( ports/port_host/src/sim_main.c ); the x86-64 port has no such command and formats a blank volume at the boot instead. fsck is the read-only check: microos> fsck fsck: 0 file(s), 3 directory(ies), 484 of 487 block(s) free fsck: the volume is consistent A broken volume prints N problem(s), the first: ... and the command exits with an error. fsck: no volume is mounted means that / is not MicroFS on this machine at the moment. /etc and the store ¶ The files of /etc are the configuration of the system, and each file is one key of the key-value store of the port (NVS on the board, a file per key in the simulator). The boot restores the files that are missing and saves the ones it finds; the file wins when the two disagree. microos> write /etc/setting hello microos> config sync config: 0 file(s) restored, 1 saved microos> config setting=hello This is why mkfs -y does not take the settings away: the store survives the volume. idf.py erase-flash destroys both. In the simulator the store is the directory MICROOS_KV_DIR ( /tmp/microos-kv by default), and a run with a volume of its own should have a store of its own too. /etc/init.d ¶ Every file of /etc/init.d is a script of the init process: one shell command per line, # starts a comment, and each script runs in a task of its own. The directory is created at the boot when it is missing. The commands are the ones of shell.md , so a script can only use what the machine registers: microos> write /etc/init.d/clock date microos> reboot Disks and partitions ¶ The kernel has a portable parser of the partition tables ( components/kernel/src/partition.c , ADR 0008 ): it reads the MBR or the GPT in the first sectors, holds every entry against the size of the disk, and registers a child device named after the parent plus p and the number of the entry. A child adds the first sector of its partition to every request and refuses what runs past its end. Device Where What flash0 board the internal flash; the mfs partition mounted at / file0 simulator a file of the host ram0 x86-64 memory, 512 KB, not persistent ata0 , ata0p1 x86-64 the IDE disk and its first partition vd0 , sd0 , nvme0n1 , mmcblk0 planned virtio, AHCI, NVMe, SDHCI Three rules of the layer matter at the console: the parser never writes to the medium: a broken table is a refusal, not a repair; a disk without a table is not a volume, and there is no "the whole disk is the filesystem" special case; what a filesystem sees is a device, so MicroFS on ata0p1 does not know that a partition table exists. The x86-64 disk is a raw 8 MB image, made by tools/x86_disk_smoke.py --mkimage and kept in build-x86/disk.img ; what is written to it survives a reset, which make x86-disk-smoke proves with two boots. See docs/ports/x86_64/README.md . The second filesystem ¶ The VFS knows filesystem types ( ADR 0009 ): vfs_register_type() puts a name and a mount function in the table, and vfs_mount_type(point, "fat32", device) mounts a type on a point. MicroFS is one type; components/fs_fat32 is a second one, FAT12/16/32 with the long names, the fixed and the cluster root and the subdirectories. The volume is read and written . It speaks the whole life of a file: open with O_CREAT , O_TRUNC and O_APPEND , write , close , unlink and mkdir , on FAT12, FAT16 and FAT32 alike. The clusters are taken from the free map and given back on removal, both copies of the table are kept together, and a long name that is created gets its run of long-name entries with the checksum of the generated 8.3 name. df works on it ( statfs walks the table), and so do the shell commands that go through the VFS: microos> write /mnt/sd/note.txt hello 6 byte(s) written to /mnt/sd/note.txt microos> cat /mnt/sd/note.txt hello mount and /etc/fstab are still ahead; an image that wants a FAT volume asks for one in its boot, after fat_vfs_register_type() . On the board the component is behind CONFIG_MICRO_OS_FS_FAT32 , off by default; the host tests always build it. What a FAT record cannot carry is still absent: stat answers mode = 0 and owner 0, chmod and chown are ENOTSUP , and there is no time of the change. unlink removes a file or an empty directory and refuses a directory that holds an entry with ENOTEMPTY ; rename is not a call of the VFS yet. The mount does not ask whether the medium can be written: a card with its physical write switch on mounts and is refused at the first write, because reading it is still useful. Writes go to the medium before the call returns and the device is synced when it has a sync of its own, but there is no journal and no fsck : a power cut in the middle of a write can leave a cluster no chain names or a half-written entry, and a checker on the host is the repair. No journal and no repair : fsck names the first problem of MicroFS, it does not fix it; FAT has no checker at all. No mv , no cp : rm -r and the other commands of the shell are there. docs.text: Micro OS has one filesystem of its own, MicroFS , two virtual filesystems, and a FAT12/16/32 volume it can both read and write. The root / is MicroFS on a block device; /proc and /dev are generated by the kernel. Everything a person writes at the console lands in MicroFS unless a FAT volume is mounted, and the configuration of /etc has a second copy in the store of the port, which is why a format does not have to lose it. The layout of the volume, the sections and the flags of a record are described in docs/memory.md ; this page is about using it.

docs.text: MicroFS is a consumer of blocks, not of a flash chip: the device under it is described by kernel/blockdev.h and registered by the port. On the board it is the mfs partition of the internal flash ( flash0 , 5.75 MB); in the simulator a file of the host ( file0 , 512 KB by default); on x86-64 the first partition of the ATA disk ( ata0p1 ) when one is attached, and a volume in the RAM ( ram0 , 512 KB) when it is not. A volume has three sections and a block is 1 KiB: Section Holds DATA the content of the files META the table of the records and the map of the free blocks INFO the header of the volume and the root record, in the last erase sector A record of today is 32 bytes: it keeps the type of the object, its mode and its owner in the upper bits of flags , and the two moments of a change ( mtime and ctime ) in the seconds of Unix after them. A volume of an older release has 16-byte records with no room for a time and mounts unchanged; its objects report zero, which is "unknown" (ADR 0013). The formatter asks for 256 records ( MFS_MOUNT_RECORDS ) and sizes META from the volume; the capacity is fixed at format time and cannot grow later. There is no journal : fsck reports the first problem it finds and does not repair, and a power cut in the middle of a write is a risk the tree knows about ( docs/debts.md ). The calls of the filesystem take one recursive lock, so two tasks can use the volume at the same time without corrupting it: each open file keeps its position in its descriptor, and the volume itself is one piece of state behind a mutex. The codes of the filesystem are translated into the codes of the system calls in one place, components/mfs/src/mfs_vfs.c .

A program asks for the moments of a change with statx (number 26 of the ABI) and microos_statx() in the library; a volume of version 1 has none, so the two times come back as zero and not as 1970. docs.text: Start here ¶ Micro OS is a Linux-like kernel for small machines. One portable core lives in components/kernel/ ; every machine is a port under it, and a board is a description of a machine plus the drivers of its chips. The same sources build as a Linux process (the unit tests and the simulator), as a bare-metal x86-64 machine in QEMU, and as the firmware of the M5Stack StickC Plus2. It is Linux- like , not Linux: the system calls are the same shape, the filesystem and the shell are the same shape, but there is no MMU on the board, no multi-user, and no dynamic linker. The x86-64 port has an MMU and uses it: a program runs in ring 3 in its own address space. The honest list of the differences is in docs/architecture.md , section 2. One kernel, four ports ¶ Port What it is Documentation ESP32 the StickC Plus2: ESP-IDF, FreeRTOS, lwIP, NVS docs/ports/esp32 x86-64 bare metal in QEMU: its own loader, ring 3 docs/ports/x86_64 host a Linux process: the tests and the simulator docs/ports/host null no machine at all: linked by the checks docs/ports/null The board is one port of several, not the project. The boundary is a contract with a version ( kernel/port/*.h , 1.6 in this tree), checked at the boot and by make integrity ; ADR 0004 explains why. What you need ¶ Need For Note cmake , ninja , gcc , python3 every host check any current Linux distribution qemu-system-x86_64 the x86-64 port optional; without it the machine is only built ESP-IDF v5.3 the firmware of the board only for make idf-* ; see build.md clang-format is needed by make format and by the format check of make integrity ; valgrind and pyserial are optional. The whole list with the packages of Arch is in commands.md . The first ten minutes ¶ From the root of the repository: make test # build the host and run the unit tests (and the null probe) make sim # boot the whole system as a process, on a volume in a file make sim is interactive: it boots the kernel, brings up MicroFS on a file volume, /proc , /dev , the configuration of /etc , the init scripts and the shell. The transcript starts like this (the version and the build date are the ones of your tree): MicroOS 0.5.0-rc1 (build ...) board: host_sim - Micro OS host simulator arch: x86_64, compiler: gcc ... port: host, contract 1.6 [ ok ] sched file0: 512 sector(s) of 1024 bytes on /tmp/microos-sim.img sim: the volume is /tmp/microos-sim.img (512 KB) [ ok ] storage ... MicroOS shell ready. Type 'help' for the list of commands. microos> Then type a few commands; leaving the input (Ctrl+D in a terminal, or the end of a pipe) ends the run: microos> uname MicroOS 0.5.0-rc1 x86_64 (build ...) microos> ls / / |-- etc/ | `-- init.d/ |-- proc/ ... microos> fsck fsck: 0 file(s), 3 directory(ies), 484 of 487 block(s) free fsck: the volume is consistent make smoke drives the same simulator with a scripted list of commands and checks the transcript; it is the end-to-end test of the host build. The other two machines ¶ The x86-64 port is the one that proves the kernel is portable, and the only machine that runs a program out of a file: make x86-build # the loader and the kernel image, in build-x86/ make x86-run # a QEMU window: VGA text and the PS/2 keyboard make x86-run-serial # the same machine on the serial console (-nographic) make x86-smoke # boot it and check the transcript, without a window The window needs a QEMU built with a display backend (the GTK one is a package of its own in some distributions); build.md has the package names and the fallbacks. A disk is optional: make x86-run-disk gives the machine an 8 MB raw image, and what it writes survives a reset. The board: make idf-build # the firmware (ESP-IDF v5.3) make idf-flash # over USB; IDF_PORT=/dev/ttyACM0 when it is not found tools/device-test.sh # build, flash, read the console, print RESULT: PASS The board comes up with the self test, the hardware doctor, the shell on the UART and a copy of it on the TFT, telnet on port 23, and the commands of the drivers ( battery , display , input , mic , wifi , ...). Where to go next ¶ build.md - the three builds in detail, and the errors that stop them. shell.md - the command line, the commands and what they print. files.md - where /etc lives, how mkfs and fsck behave. programs.md - what exec needs and which machine can run it. ports.md - the differences between the four machines at a glance. What this is not yet ¶ A short list, so that nothing here reads as a promise: No MMU on the board, no memory protection. The user/kernel split is logical; fork() shares the memory of the parent and re-enters the program. Programs run on x86-64 only. The board's flash is not executable for a file and the simulator must not jump into an arbitrary image, so execve answers ENOSYS there. One user, uid 0. A file has a mode and an owner, and the mode is checked, but there is no group and no second user. FAT32 is read-only, ext2 is not there. MicroFS is the root of the tree; a build can also carry a reader of FAT12/16/32 ( ADR 0009 ) and mount it beside MicroFS. MicroFS has the two moments of a change and no journal; FAT keeps no time yet, and writing to FAT, ext2 and a second FAT volume are still ahead. docs/debts.md keeps the full register with the next step of each row. docs/roadmap.md is the plan. docs.text: Kernel and ABI ¶ The system calls are the only door between a program and the kernel. Their numbers are a contract : they are written down, covered by a test, and never change. A program built for one version of the kernel keeps working with the next one. The canonical document, with the arguments and the reasoning, is docs/syscall-abi.md ; this page is the map for a person who wants to use the system, not a second copy of the contract. The table ¶ No. Call What it does 0 exit end the task (or the program) with a status 1 read bytes out of a descriptor 2 write bytes into a descriptor 3 open a descriptor for a path, with flags 4 close drop a descriptor 5 stat the type, the mode, the owner, the size 6 lseek move the position of a descriptor 7 unlink remove a file 8 mkdir create a directory 9 readdir the next entries of a directory 10 getpid the number of the task 11 getcwd the current directory 12 ioctl a command of a device 13 yield give the processor away 14 sleep wait in milliseconds 15 uptime milliseconds since the boot 16 reboot restart the machine 17 fork a child task 18 getppid the number of the parent 19 waitpid wait for a child, get its status 20 malloc memory of the kernel heap 21 free give it back 22 realloc resize a block 23 chmod the mode of an object 24 chown the owner of an object 25 execve make the caller a program 26 statx the numbers of stat and the moments of a change 27 is the count, not a call. A number that is not in the table is ENOSYS ; a new call always takes the next free number, and an old one never moves. The shell prints the same table with abi : microos> abi the system calls of the kernel: nr name 0 exit ... 25 execve 26 statx 27 call(s) registered The convention is the one of Linux: the number and six arguments, the result in the return value, and a negative result is an error with the number of POSIX ( -14 is EFAULT , -2 is ENOENT , -38 is ENOSYS ). The width of an argument is the width of a pointer of the machine: 32 bits on the board, 64 bits on the host and on x86-64. The edge of the table ¶ Every argument is checked where it enters, in components/kernel/src/ksys.c , before a filesystem or a driver sees it: a path is not NULL, begins at / , and ends within 127 characters ( KSYS_PATH_MAX , one less than VFS_PATH_MAX ); a path that does not end in the window is ENAMETOOLONG ; a buffer is NULL only with a zero length, and no call touches more than 64 KiB in one exchange; a longer one is E2BIG , a NULL with a length is EINVAL ; the memory of the caller is checked through the port: on a machine with paging the kernel walks the page tables of the program, and a range that is not there is EFAULT ; the bytes are then copied with copy_from_user() / copy_to_user() , so the VFS never sees a pointer of the program; the flags of open are one of the three access modes and no bit outside the contract; the whence of lseek and the pid of waitpid are compared before a cast can cut a wide register into a valid value; stat and getcwd need the place for the answer: NULL is EINVAL , a place that is not the caller's memory is EFAULT ; readdir takes whole entries: a count that is not a multiple of the size of an entry is EINVAL . EFAULT is the most interesting of them, because it is what a machine with an MMU can finally say. On x86-64 the null page, the guard page under the stack, the part of the window that was never mapped and a range that runs past 0x03000000 are all "not there": the call answers -14 instead of taking a page fault in ring 0. /bin/badptr is the program of that test - it hands write , stat and read a pointer outside the window, a range that crosses its end and the guard page, and every call answers 14 while the machine goes on and writes a line with a valid pointer afterwards. Descriptors ¶ Every task has a table of four descriptors, and the descriptor is the number of the slot. A descriptor remembers the access it was opened with: reading one opened for writing, or writing one opened for reading, is EBADF before a filesystem is asked. The position of a file lives in the descriptor, not in the filesystem, so two tasks do not move each other's cursor. A directory is opened with KSYS_O_DIRECTORY ( 0x0800 ) and read with readdir ; it is read, never written. A plain open of a directory is EISDIR , and readdir of a file is ENOTDIR . The mode and the owner ¶ Every object has nine bits of rwx and a uid of fifteen bits, stored in the spare bits of its MicroFS record ( docs/memory.md ). A new file is 0644 , a new directory 0755 , and the owner is 0. The system has one user , uid 0, and it gets no exemption of root : a file of mode 0200 cannot be read by the only user of the system either. An object owned by uid 0 is judged by the triad of the owner, one owned by any other number by the triad of the others, because there is no group here. open compares its access with the mode before a descriptor exists, so every filesystem answers a forbidden open the same way ( EPERM ); execve needs the x bit; stat reports and checks nothing, as in POSIX. A mode outside the nine bits and an owner outside the fifteen are EINVAL , not a number cut to fit. chmod 000 is not expressible: a zero in the record means "this record predates the modes", so the filesystem refuses it instead of writing a number it would read back as 0644 . The x bit of every directory of a path is walked and checked before the object at the end: a directory of mode 0600 keeps its children out of reach of open , stat and execve . docs.text: Ports ¶ A port is a directory that implements the contract of kernel/port/*.h ; a board is a description of a machine plus the drivers of its chips. The kernel in components/kernel/ includes nothing of a platform, and make integrity fails when it tries. That is why the same sources build as a Linux process, as a bare-metal x86-64 machine and as the firmware of the board; the reasoning is in ADR 0004 , and the recipe for a new machine is in docs/porting.md . What runs where ¶ yes means it is there and used, - means it is absent, and a note in parentheses is the reason. ESP32 (board) x86-64 (QEMU) host (simulator) null shell UART and TFT VGA, PS/2, COM1 stdin/stdout - MicroFS the mfs partition, 5.75 MB the disk, or 512 KB of RAM a file, 512 KB - /proc , /dev yes yes yes - /etc and its store files, NVS behind them files, no store files, a file per key - execve ENOSYS (no executable flash) ring 3, own page tables ENOSYS (a harness) ENOSYS fork() shared memory copy on write shared memory shared memory disk the internal flash ATA PIO, ata0 - - network WiFi, lwIP, telnet, HTTP, MQTT - - - panel ST7789v2 and a copy of the console VGA text a renderer into a file - MMU - (the chip has none) yes, used for programs - - build make idf-build make x86-build make build by the host build The matrix follows the ports, not a wish: the board has no MMU and its flash is not executable for a file, so it cannot run a program; the simulator must not jump into an arbitrary image, so it cannot either; the x86-64 machine has the loader, the page tables and the ring that make it possible. Everything else - the scheduler, the VFS, MicroFS, /proc , /dev , the libc subset, the shell - is the same code on all of them. ESP32: the board ¶ The M5Stack StickC Plus2 ( ESP32-PICO-V3-02 , 240 MHz, 2 MB PSRAM, 8 MB flash, 135x240 TFT), on ESP-IDF v5.3 and FreeRTOS. make idf-build make idf-flash IDF_PORT = /dev/ttyACM0 tools/device-test.sh /dev/ttyACM0 # build, flash, read, RESULT: PASS What works: the boot with the self test and the hardware doctor, the console on the UART and on the TFT, MicroFS on the flash, /log/start.log , the scripts of /etc/init.d , the drivers (display, buttons, buzzer, LED, IMU, RTC, battery, microphone, WiFi), telnet on port 23, httpd , mqtt , http and ntp . What does not: memory protection ( fork() is the placeholder of a machine without an MMU), running a program out of the flash, OTA, the IR driver, the sound detector, the enclosure modes, a second user. The RTC alarm turns the board on from off; it does not wake a chip that is already asleep (the INT is wired to the power latch, the notes say so). The flash is 8 MB: factory 2 MB and MicroFS 5.75 MB, with no OTA slot. The details, the pins and the quirks are in docs/ports/esp32/README.md and docs/ports/esp32/hardware.md . x86-64: bare metal in QEMU ¶ A machine with no operating system under it: no libc, no POSIX, no firmware. The loader is a multiboot image that QEMU takes with -kernel ; it copies the kernel to 16 MiB, builds the identity map of the first gigabyte and turns long mode on. make x86-build make x86-run # the window: VGA text and the PS/2 keyboard make x86-run-serial # the same machine in a terminal make x86-smoke # boot and check the transcript What works: the VGA text console and COM1 out of one k_port_write() , the PS/2 keyboard, the PIT, the context switch, the scheduler, paging and ring 3, execve with MOX1 images, fork() with copy on write, MicroFS on the first partition of an ATA disk (or on 512 KB of RAM without one), the modes and the owners. It is the machine of programs.md and the proof that the kernel is portable. What does not: the network ( k_port_net_* says no), the key-value store (no /etc to persist), a second disk, DMA, the kernel in a higher half. The details are in docs/ports/x86_64/README.md . host: the tests and the simulator ¶ A Linux process: threads instead of a scheduler substrate, pthread mutexes instead of a spinlock, files and sockets instead of a flash and a radio. It is the development loop and the machine of make test . make test # the unit tests, plus the null probe make sim # the whole system on a volume in a file make smoke # the same, driven by a script What works: everything portable, with the drivers stubbed and the console rendered into a file or nowhere. What it cannot do: run a program, and reproduce preemption - the critical section is a recursive pthread mutex, so a race is invisible unless the race detector looks for it ( make test-tsan ). The details are in docs/ports/host/README.md . null: the port that is not a machine ¶ ports/port_null answers "there is no such thing" to every call: no console, no flash, no store, no sockets, no tasks. It is never run for a purpose. It exists for one check: microos_null_probe links the kernel and every portable component against it, so a symbol that portable code takes from a machine by accident stops the build on a laptop. It is compiled by the host build and run by ctest , and it is the compiled form of ADR 0004. It cannot catch a libc call - the probe is linked with the libc of the host - but it catches a leak of the port itself, which is the part that has to be complete. The details are in docs/ports/null/README.md . docs.text: Programs ¶ A program in Micro OS is a file , not a function of the kernel: execve reads the file through the VFS, the kernel checks it against a format of its own, and the port places it in memory and enters it. The decisions are in ADR 0005 (the format and the rights), ADR 0006 (the entry) and ADR 0007 (the address space and ring 3); the report of the phase is docs/phases/phase7.md . Only one machine of the tree can run a program: Machine k_port_exec_supported() What execve answers x86-64 in QEMU true it runs the image in ring 3 ESP32 board false ENOSYS (the flash is not executable for a file) host simulator false ENOSYS (a test harness must not jump into an image) null port false ENOSYS On the board and in the simulator the shell still has exec ; it looks for the file, checks the execute bit, and then reports that this machine cannot run a program. That is the contract working, not a missing build. The format: MOX1 ¶ An executable is a flat image: a header of 32 bytes, then the code, then the initialised data. The bss is not in the file; the port clears it. The layout is in components/kernel/include/kernel/exec.h : Offset Field Meaning 0 magic the bytes M , O , X , 1 4 version 1 8 flags 0; a flag the kernel does not know is a refusal 12 entry the offset of the first instruction, from the start of the image 16 text_size the bytes of code 20 data_size the bytes of initialised data 24 bss_size the bytes to clear, at most 1 MiB 28 reserved 0 32 the text, then the data The parser ( components/kernel/src/exec.c ) checks the image against itself and nothing else: the magic and the version, the sizes against the file, a text that is not empty, an entry inside the text, sizes that are multiples of four, a known flag, and a bss under a megabyte. Whether the image fits the window of the machine is the port's question, asked later. tools/mkprog.sh turns a linked object into an image: tools/mkprog.sh [ --base 0x02000000 ] hello.elf hello.mox hello_main The image is not relocated: the code and the data have to be linked for the address the port names, and --base makes the script refuse an image linked for another window. The x86-64 port builds its four programs this way: the object is compiled for the window, linked with programs/program.ld , turned into a .mox by the script and embedded in the kernel as a blob, because the kernel needs the bytes before it has a filesystem to read them from. /bin and the boot ¶ The x86-64 port mounts MicroFS at / , creates /bin , writes four images there and gives them the mode of a program ( 0755 ) through the VFS: File What it proves /bin/hello the door: write , arguments, pid, clock, sleep , exit ; it prints cpl 3 /bin/crash a fault of ring 3 is reported and the shell survives /bin/fork fork() with copy on write: the child gets 0, the parent the pid /bin/badptr a pointer outside the window is EFAULT , not a fault of ring 0 The boot then asks for /bin/hello with ksys_execve() : the stat, the check of the mode, the read through the VFS, the parse and the entry are the ones of the call and not a copy of them. The shell runs the same file with exec . exec at the console ¶ microos> exec hello PROGRAM: hello from /bin PROGRAM: cpl 3 PROGRAM: argc 1, argv[0] hello PROGRAM: pid 4, up 2869 ms PROGRAM: slept 10 ms, up 2880 ms the program has finished microos> exec crash PROGRAM: crash writes to address zero the program faulted: vector 14 at 0x0000000000000000 the program has finished A name with a slash is a path; a name without one is looked up in PATH , where the first regular file with an execute bit wins. The vector of the arguments is the line after the name, with argv[0] the name that was typed, as in Linux. The port also prints the lines of the task ( task: created 'program' ... , x86-64: the program exited with 0 ); they are left out here. The shell waits: execve returns only when the program has ended (or when it never started), and the port prints the status the program ended with (0 to 255). The errors, in the order they are met: Answer Reason ENOENT the path names nothing EISDIR it is a directory EPERM the file has no x bit for the caller ( 0400 is not a program) EINVAL the file is not a MOX1 image of this system ENOMEM the image does not fit the window of the port ENOSYS this machine has no window of programs A failed execve spends no descriptor of the caller: the file is read through the VFS, not through the table of the task. The entry: int $0x80 ¶ A program of x86-64 is not a function of the kernel, so the call has to be an instruction of the processor. docs.text: A program in Micro OS is a file , not a function of the kernel: execve reads the file through the VFS, the kernel checks it against a format of its own, and the port places it in memory and enters it. The decisions are in ADR 0005 (the format and the rights), ADR 0006 (the entry) and ADR 0007 (the address space and ring 3); the report of the phase is docs/phases/phase7.md . Only one machine of the tree can run a program: Machine k_port_exec_supported() What execve answers x86-64 in QEMU true it runs the image in ring 3 ESP32 board false ENOSYS (the flash is not executable for a file) host simulator false ENOSYS (a test harness must not jump into an image) null port false ENOSYS On the board and in the simulator the shell still has exec ; it looks for the file, checks the execute bit, and then reports that this machine cannot run a program. docs.text: An executable is a flat image: a header of 32 bytes, then the code, then the initialised data. The bss is not in the file; the port clears it. The layout is in components/kernel/include/kernel/exec.h : Offset Field Meaning 0 magic the bytes M , O , X , 1 4 version 1 8 flags 0; a flag the kernel does not know is a refusal 12 entry the offset of the first instruction, from the start of the image 16 text_size the bytes of code 20 data_size the bytes of initialised data 24 bss_size the bytes to clear, at most 1 MiB 28 reserved 0 32 the text, then the data The parser ( components/kernel/src/exec.c ) checks the image against itself and nothing else: the magic and the version, the sizes against the file, a text that is not empty, an entry inside the text, sizes that are multiples of four, a known flag, and a bss under a megabyte. The x86-64 port builds its four programs this way: the object is compiled for the window, linked with programs/program.ld , turned into a .mox by the script and embedded in the kernel as a blob, because the kernel needs the bytes before it has a filesystem to read them from.

docs.text: The shell ¶ Every boot ends at a prompt: MicroOS shell ready. Type 'help' for the list of commands. microos> The shell is components/kshell , part of the kernel: the same interpreter and the same commands on the board, in the simulator and on x86-64. A port or a driver adds commands of its own by registering them by name, which is why the list is not the same on every machine. The line ¶ The line is split on spaces and tabs; there are no quotes, no escapes, no globs, no pipes, no ; and no redirection. A line is at most 127 characters and at most 8 words. Backspace erases, Ctrl+C throws the line away, and a line that did not fit is not executed (the shell says line too long, it was not executed ), because a cut line is a different command. Because there are no quotes, a command that needs an empty argument accepts the two characters "" as the way to type it. path "" is the example. A name that is not registered answers <name>: command not found . A command that is given the wrong arguments answers with its own usage: line and does nothing. help ¶ microos> help command what it does mkfs format the volume: mkfs -y ... microos> help exec exec: run a program: exec <program> [args...] help with an argument prints the same text as <command> --help : the usage line, the summary and the notes. help --help explains help itself. Options and -h / --help ¶ Every command answers -h and --help without running: a usage: line, the summary from the table of the commands and the notes of the command. The flag has to be the first word of the line; a -h deeper in the arguments is a character the command sees. -- ends the options, so a name that starts with - can still be passed. A command that does not have a flag refuses it: ls -z prints ls: unknown option: -z and the usage line. df -h is the one GNU-shaped exception: -h asks for human sizes, so the help of df is df --help . The commands ¶ The core of the kernel, on every machine: Command What it does help [command] the list of commands, or the full help of one uname the name, the version, the architecture and the build id uptime the time since the boot, the ticks and the task count ps the tasks: pid, priority, state, name free the memory of the heap and of the PSRAM dmesg the log of the boot, from the ring buffer of the kernel echo <words> print the words sleep <milliseconds> wait, up to 60000 clear clear the screen (the escape sequence the panel and the VGA read) modules run the hardware doctor and print its report abi the table of the system calls memtest [kilobytes] measure the memory and its speed mfetch [color] the system report with a logo reboot restart the machine The files, on every machine: Command What it does pwd , cd <dir> the current directory ls [-l] [-a] [path] the tree; -l adds mode, owner and size, -a the hidden . and .. cat [-n] <file> the content of a file; -n numbers the lines write <file> <text> create or replace a file with one line (at most 127 bytes) mkdir <dir> , rm [-r] <file> a directory, a file; a directory needs -r df [-h] [path] the free blocks and inodes; -h in KB/MB mount the mounted filesystems fsck check the volume, read-only stat <path> the type, the mode, the owner and the size chmod <mode> <path> , chown <uid> <path> the mode (octal) and the owner (0..32767) path [directories] show or set PATH exec <program> [args...] run a program, by a path or found in PATH The services, where the port registers them: Command What it does Where config , config sync list the store of /etc , restore and save it board, simulator mkfs -y format the volume (erases everything) board, simulator http get <url> one HTTP request; prints the status and the body board ntp [server] set the clock from NTP (UTC), default pool.ntp.org board httpd [port\|off] the page of the state over HTTP, default port 80 board mqtt <host> <port> <topic> <message> publish one message at QoS 0 board telnet [on\|off] the shell on port 23 board date , date set <YYYY-MM-DD> <HH:MM:SS> the RTC, or the clock of the host board, simulator battery , beep [frequency] [ms] , led on\|off\|heart\|dance the power cell, the buzzer, the LED board, simulator (stubs) input [seconds] watch the buttons board, simulator (stubs) wifi [status\|scan\|connect <ssid> [key]\|join\|disconnect\|forget] the WiFi station board, simulator (stub) display [<x> <y>] \| rotate <0\|90\|180\|270> \| invert [on\|off] \| draw [seconds] the panel board i2c scan the I2C bus board mic the level of the microphone board rtc alarm [HH:MM\|+<seconds>\|day <1-31> HH:MM\|clear] the alarm of the BM8563 and its flag board power [sleep <seconds>\|off] deep sleep with the timer or button C, or power off board factory reset -y erase MicroFS and the NVS, then restart; without -y it only explains board The simulator has no network and no drivers: http , ntp , httpd , mqtt and telnet are not registered there at all, and the driver commands of the board are stubs that answer something sensible. The x86-64 port registers only the core and the files: no config , no mkfs , no date , no network. This is the port boundary doing its job, not a bug; ports.md has the whole matrix. PATH and exec ¶ PATH starts at /bin:/usr/bin and belongs to the shell: it is not a file of /etc , and a program does not inherit it yet. microos> path /bin:/usr/bin microos> path /bin microos> path "" A name with a slash is a path and is used as it is. A name without one is looked up in PATH , and the first regular file with an execute bit wins; a file without the bit is passed over, as in Linux. A search that found nothing says where it looked: microos> exec hello exec: hello: not found in /bin:/usr/bin On the board and in the simulator there is no program to run: a fresh volume has no /bin , and execve answers ENOSYS even for a file that is there. The x86-64 port writes /bin/hello , /bin/crash , /bin/fork and /bin/badptr at the boot, and runs them as programs of ring 3. programs.md explains what a program is. stat , chmod and chown ¶ Every object has a mode of nine bits and an owner, a uid of fifteen bits. A new file is 0644 , a new directory 0755 , and the owner is 0. stat prints the line of ls -l first and then the same numbers as fields: microos> stat /etc drwxr-xr-x 0 14 /etc type: directory mode: 0755 owner: 0 size: 14 An object of a filesystem that keeps no modes ( /proc , /dev , or a volume written by an older release) prints mode: (not set) and no ls line: nine dashes would read as 0000 , which is a statement the record does not make. chmod takes an octal mode, chown a uid: microos> chmod 0700 /etc/init.d microos> chown 0 /etc/setting microos> chmod 0755 /bin/hello A mode that is not octal ( 0999 ), a uid above 32767 and a missing path are refused with a sentence. chmod 000 is not a way to lock a file: the filesystem keeps a zero as "this record predates the modes", so it refuses the call instead of storing a number it would read back as 0644 . fsck and mkfs ¶ fsck reads the volume and reports; it never repairs. microos> fsck fsck: 0 file(s), 3 directory(ies), 484 of 487 block(s) free fsck: the volume is consistent A volume with a problem prints the count and the first problem and exits with an error. fsck: no volume is mounted means what it says: there is no MicroFS at / on this machine right now. mkfs -y unmounts the volume, formats it and mounts it again. The -y is mandatory: everything in MicroFS is destroyed. The files of /etc come back from the store of the port at the next boot (or at config sync ), because the configuration keeps a copy outside the filesystem; the rest does not come back. On the board idf.py erase-flash destroys the store as well. httpd : the page of the state ¶ httpd opens a small HTTP server on the machine. It is not started by the boot: a machine of this size opens a port when its owner says so, from the shell or from a script of /etc/init.d . microos> httpd httpd: the page is on port 80 microos> httpd 8080 httpd: already on port 80 microos> httpd off httpd: stopped Request Answer GET / the name, version, architecture, uptime, memory, PSRAM and task count GET /health ok (a page of plain text, for a script) any other path 404 Not Found a method other than GET 405 Method Not Allowed Moving the server is httpd off and then httpd <port> : a second httpd with a port only says where the page already is. A port that is not ours is reported and the server stays off. mqtt : one message ¶ The MQTT client is 3.1.1 at QoS 0 and 1. The shell command publishes one message and disconnects; it is a way to send a word to a broker from a script or from the console, not a client that lives in the board. microos> mqtt 10.10.10.1 1883 home/board hello mqtt: 5 byte(s) to home/board on 10.10.10.1:1883 The limits are the ones of mqtt.h : a topic of 128 bytes, a payload of 256, a client id of 32, a session timeout of five seconds. There is no TLS: the broker has to be on the network of the owner. A refused client and a broker that does not answer are different sentences, so the console says which one happened. telnet and config ¶ telnet puts the shell on port 23 beside the UART and the panel; the negotiation is answered with refusals and the client keeps its own echo. There is no authentication, and telnet off closes the door. config lists the store of /etc (the key-value store of the port, NVS on the board), and config sync restores the files that are missing and saves the ones that are there. The file wins when the two disagree — see files.md . The commands of a script ¶ Every file of /etc/init.d is a script of the init process: one shell command per line, # starts a comment, and each script runs in a task of its own. This is how a service of the board starts without a person at the console: microos> mkdir /etc/init.d microos> write /etc/init.d/clock date microos> reboot The commands of the script are the commands of this page, so a script can only use what the machine registers. A line that fails is reported in the log and does not stop the other lines of the script. Back to the wiki index

There is no TLS: the broker has to be on the network of the owner. A refused client and a broker that does not answer are different sentences, so the console says which one happened.
docs.title: mqtt: one message

docs.text: telnet puts the shell on port 23 beside the UART and the panel; the negotiation is answered with refusals and the client keeps its own echo. There is no authentication, and telnet off closes the door. config lists the store of /etc (the key-value store of the port, NVS on the board), and config sync restores the files that are missing and saves the ones that are there. The file wins when the two disagree — see files.md .
docs.title: telnet and config

docs.text: Every file of /etc/init.d is a script of the init process: one shell command per line, # starts a comment, and each script runs in a task of its own. This is how a service of the board starts without a person at the console: microos> mkdir /etc/init.d microos> write /etc/init.d/clock date microos> reboot The commands of the script are the commands of this page, so a script can only use what the machine registers. A line that fails is reported in the log and does not stop the other lines of the script. Back to the wiki index

docs.text: Testing ¶ The checks are layered by what they can see. A unit test sees one piece of the kernel; the simulator sees the whole portable system as a process; the x86-64 smoke test sees a bare machine and a processor; the device test sees the board and the chips on it. None of them replaces another. The commands ¶ Command What it proves Needs make test the host build, the unit tests, the null probe gcc , cmake , ninja make test-asan the same tests with the sanitizers the same make test-tsan the same tests under the race detector the same make test-minimal the host tests with the optional features off the same make smoke the simulator boots and the shell answers the host build make x86-build the x86-64 kernel and loader compile gcc , cmake , ninja make x86-smoke the kernel boots, runs /bin/hello , the shell answers qemu-system-x86_64 make x86-vga-smoke the VGA screen and the PS/2 keyboard, no display qemu-system-x86_64 make x86-disk-smoke a file written by one boot is read by the next qemu-system-x86_64 make integrity the boundary, the bundle, the partitions, the hygiene clang-format make ci the list a contributor runs before a push the above, QEMU optional tools/device-test.sh build, flash and boot the board ESP-IDF and a board make test : the unit tests ¶ make test configures and builds build-host/ and runs ctest , which runs three tests: microos_tests - the unit tests, in tests/cases/ , on the framework of tests/framework/ktest.h . There is no external dependency; the tests run inside a real kernel task, so they exercise the task API as well. mkprog - tools/test_mkprog.py , the layout of the image that tools/mkprog.sh writes; it builds tiny objects with the compiler of the host and skips itself when Python is not found. null_probe - the kernel and every portable component linked against the null port. A symbol that portable code takes from a machine by accident is a link error here, on a laptop. The numeric corpus is tests/corpus/vectors.txt : 512 numbers with the boundary values (0, 1, 255, 65535, 2147483647 and so on) mixed in. A new numeric behaviour reuses it rather than inventing a second list. make test-asan and make test-tsan are the same tests in build-asan/ and build-tsan/ . The board has no debugger, so the host is the place where a wrong pointer or undefined behaviour has to be caught; TSan is the only thing that sees a race, because the host port cannot reproduce preemption. make test-minimal is the second configuration of the host build (ADR 0010): KERNEL_PSRAM , KERNEL_EXEC , the network components and the second filesystem are off, in build-minimal/ . It proves that the sources still build without them and runs the tests that do not need the feature - the cases of exec and of the network are guarded in the source, so the report still says how many checks the small build has. make smoke : the simulator ¶ make smoke runs tools/sim_smoke.py , which boots build-host/ports/port_host/microos_sim with a volume and a store of its own, types a list of commands and checks the transcript: the subsystems, MicroFS, /proc , /dev , the configuration of /etc , the shell. It is the cheapest end-to-end test of the portable system, and it takes a couple of seconds. make sim runs the same binary by hand, with /tmp/microos-sim.img and /tmp/microos-kv by default. python3 tools/sim_smoke.py --verbose shows every step. The x86-64 smoke tests ¶ make x86-smoke boots the kernel on a real (emulated) processor: QEMU loads the loader of the port, the loader turns long mode on and copies the kernel, and the kernel prints its banner on the serial port. Then the script types commands into COM1 and checks the answers: the boot, the filesystem, the program of /bin (the execve path, the arguments, the status), the fork with copy on write, the fault of /bin/crash , and the EFAULT of /bin/badptr . The run of this tree passes 48 checks and ends with RESULT: PASS . make x86-vga-smoke looks at the other console: it boots with -display none , reads the text memory at 0xB8000 through the monitor of QEMU, takes a screenshot and types with sendkey , so it proves the screen and IRQ1 without a display server. It is a target of its own and not a part of make ci : the monitor of QEMU is a tool a build farm does not have to have. make x86-disk-smoke gives the machine an 8 MB image on the primary IDE channel, writes a file in one boot and reads it in the next. It is the test of the ATA driver, of the MBR parser and of MicroFS on a real medium, and it is also not a part of make ci . make integrity : the boundary and the hygiene ¶ tools/integrity_check.py checks what a compiler cannot: the layers : the kernel includes only the kernel, a portable component no platform header and no k_port_* call, and a port implements the whole contract of kernel/port/*.h ; the bundle in dist/ , when there is one: the sums and the images; the partition table : partitions.csv against the flash size and the build; the budget of the image: the firmware fits its 2 MB slot; the features (ADR 0010): a flag that is off leaves no symbol in the map of the ESP-IDF build and no library in the host build; git : the objects, through git fsck --strict ; the hygiene of the sources: UTF-8, LF, no trailing whitespace, no tabs, 100 columns in C, and clang-format when it is installed. --skip-format --skip-git and --expect-version <version> are the useful options when a release is prepared; --verbose names every check. make ci : the local half ¶ build, test, test-asan, test-tsan, smoke, [x86-smoke], integrity x86-smoke joins the list when qemu-system-x86_64 is on PATH and is skipped with a message when it is not: a missing optional machine must not fail a run. make ci does not build the firmware of the board (that needs ESP-IDF) and does not run the VGA or disk smoke tests or the device test. The cloud repeats the list on every push to mainline and release_candidate and adds what a build farm has: valgrind over the tests, the firmware build, the bundle, and x86-smoke . The local half and the cloud half are close but not identical; docs/debts.md keeps the difference as a debt. The device test ¶ tools/device-test.sh # auto-detected port tools/device-test.sh /dev/ttyACM0 CONSOLE_SECONDS = 60 tools/device-test.sh /dev/ttyACM0 The script finds ESP-IDF ( $IDF_PATH , ../esp-idf , ~/esp/esp-idf ), builds, flashes, reads the console for CONSOLE_SECONDS (30 by default) and prints RESULT: PASS when the self test, the hardware doctor and the shell came up. It is outside CI: no runner has the board. A release is gated on it by hand. tools/console.py reads the console without flashing; tools/stream_console.py is the interactive version. Both need pyserial , which the ESP-IDF Python environment already has. Adding a test ¶ A new case needs four touches (the same list as in AGENTS.md ): tests/cases/test_<thing>.c ; the void test_<thing>(void); declaration in tests/include/tests/tests.h ; the call in run_tests() in tests/src/main.c ; the file in add_executable(microos_tests ...) in tests/CMakeLists.txt . Kernel behaviour without a test is unfinished work. A test that needs real hardware is a sign that platform and portable code got mixed: the kernel tests run on the host, and the board is checked by the device test and by the smoke tests of its port. The fuzz of the ABI and of MOX1 has a deterministic seed ( tests/cases/test_fuzz.c ); the records of MicroFS have none yet, which is an open row of the register. Back to the wiki index
